criterion_notes.c1: Examines rural household domestic and irrigation water access (including piped water in the compound, time and distance to domestic water source, sanitation facility, and household water security/poverty status).
criterion_notes.c2: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 but fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, the study examines an institutional/governance factor because Water Resource Users Associations (WRUAs) are localized collective-action water governance bodies institutionalized under Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016 (and land title is included as a covariate). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, however, the empirical exposure is simply binary household participation in community-based water development projects / collective action (WRUA membership vs. non-membership), with the Water Acts serving only as unanalysed macro-governance background. The study does not analyze any rule-type mechanism directly governing service access—such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements for service connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure. Land title is treated as a farm wealth/tenure-security incentive predicting voluntary group participation (and is embedded inside the Capacity sub-index of the composite Water Poverty Index), not as a tenure requirement governing water service access.
criterion_notes.c3: Quantitative empirical study using primary household survey data collected between September and December 2019 from 652 randomly sampled rural households, analyzed with full-information maximum likelihood endogenous switching probit (ESP), propensity score matching (PSM), and inverse probability weighting (IPW).
criterion_notes.c4: Models binary household water poverty status (40th percentile of a polychoric PCA Water Poverty Index incorporating water availability, reliability, piped water, and sanitation accessibility alongside capacity, uses, and environment components) and descriptively compares piped water in the compound, time and distance to domestic water source, traditional latrine without roof, and irrigation water access between WRUA members and non-members (note that main water source variables are also treated as selection instruments predicting WRUA membership).
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (652 rural smallholder farming households in 8 sub-catchments of the Upper Ewaso Ng'iro North Catchment Area, Kenya; household unit), exposure (binary WRUA / community-based water development project membership), outcomes (binary consumption poverty, income poverty, subjective poverty, and composite water poverty status), and cross-sectional econometric design are clearly specified.

evidence_quotes.quote: Collective action has been taken up following the International Water Management (IWM) principles and institutionalized in the Kenyan legal framework through water resource users’ associations (WRUAs). We carried out this study to assess whether this collective action has any impact on household poverty using objective poverty measures (consumption and income), a subjective poverty measure and a water poverty measure.

The Kenyan water policy framework recognizes WRUAs as the legal, grassroots collective action organ entrusted with water resources management, allocation and control through the Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016.

The ATU results imply that non-members would have significant reductions in household poverty if they considered membership into Community-Based Water Development Projects in this case WRUA, whereby, they would have reduced consumption poverty by about 6%, reduced income poverty by about 25%, reduced subjective poverty by about 12% and reduced water poverty by about 11%.
Data were collected in the period between September 2019 and December 2019 from a sample of 652 households. Multistage sampling technique was employed in the study.
With regards to water, members have better access to both domestic and irrigation water, whereby, more members have piped water supply in their compound.
We therefore used the 40th percentile of the household water poverty index as the water poverty cut-off line to generate a water poverty dummy where Water poor = 1, and Water non-poor = 0.

raw_response.exposure: Household membership in a Water Resource Users Association (WRUA) / community-based water development project (CWDP) (binary collective-action participation indicator).
raw_response.outcome: Binary household consumption poverty, income poverty, subjective poverty (Economic Ladder Question), and composite water poverty status (40th percentile of household Water Poverty Index), plus descriptive differences in piped water in compound, time/distance to domestic water source, sanitation facility, and irrigation water access.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Rural smallholder farming households in eight sub-catchments of the Upper Ewaso Ng'iro North Catchment Area, Kenya; cross-sectional sample of 652 households (331 WRUA members and 321 non-members; household unit of analysis).
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 rule-type scope clarification for Criterion 2. Although the study examines rural household water security/poverty and water access indicators using 2019 survey data from 652 smallholder households in Kenya, its exposure is generic participation in community-based water development projects / collective action (WRUA membership vs. non-membership), with Kenya's Water Act 2002 and Water Act 2016 serving only as unanalysed macro-governance background. No rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules for water connection, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) is empirically examined. Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included because WRUAs are institutionalized local water governance associations.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional observational household survey analyzed using full-information maximum likelihood endogenous switching probit (ESP), propensity score matching (PSM), and inverse probability weighting (IPW).
